title: 10+ years trading manually, two months into automation: my Gold system research and what the tests did not prove
author: symtrader
selftext:
Hi everyone. I've traded Gold and Nasdaq manually for over ten years, but I only started trying to automate my approach around two months ago. Surprisingly, Gold has been easier to translate so far. I expected Nasdaq to be simpler, but I still haven't captured that system satisfactorily.

I started by recording myself explaining charts, including market structure, candle bodies and wicks. Then I developed a TradingView indicator to mark my setups and compared its decisions with my chart reading as new candles formed. Making the rules explicit exposed ambiguities that had felt obvious when trading manually.

I've been using Claude and Codex to help with implementation. My first approach sent TradingView signals through PineConnector to MT5. Delays and execution costs mattered more than I expected. Negotiating lower broker fees helped, and the experience pushed me toward a native MT5 implementation. An earlier experimental algo running on a small live account has taught me about restart recovery and execution, but its results are separate from the research below.

The current candidate is Vesper 2.1. AI is helping me develop and test the software, rather than being asked to improvise trade decisions. Native implementation and validation are still in progress. I'm sharing the research process and its limitations without publishing the entry rules or source code.

This post covers the Gold only research version. It does not combine results from different instruments, risk settings or versions into one performance curve.

# What the system does

It translates a discretionary trading framework into repeatable decisions, with defined entry eligibility, position sizing and trade management. The portfolio has several components sharing account equity and margin. The simulation accounts for percentage risk budgets, monthly equity based sizing, minimum lot sizes, volume rounding, position limits and trading costs.

I am keeping the actual signals, thresholds, filters and management rules private. The useful part to share is how the system was evaluated and where that evaluation still falls short.

# The historical result

Period: January 1, 2017 through October 15, 2026.  
Starting capital: $10,000, compounded continuously across the period with monthly sizing updates.  
Instrument: Gold CFD.  
Data: reconstructed historical research feed, not native broker tick execution.

Primary modeled outcome:

Ending equity: $284,565.64.  
Net modeled profit: $274,565.64.  
Total return: 2,745.66 percent across the entire period, not an annual return.  
Accepted trades: 621.  
Win rate: 35.27 percent.  
Profit factor: 1.80, calculated from modeled dollar trade profits and losses.  
Maximum floating drawdown: 28.18 percent.

These are simulated account results. They are not live profits, verified broker statements or cash withdrawals. The curve retains profits and compounds them, so it is not an income or payout illustration. Taxes are excluded, and historical execution and financing are assumptions.

# What happened when execution got worse

Primary: ending equity $284,565.64, maximum floating drawdown 28.18 percent, 621 trades.  
Harsh: ending equity $103,703.08, maximum floating drawdown 31.69 percent, 410 trades.  
Extreme: ending equity $49,521.92, maximum floating drawdown 41.24 percent, 368 trades.

Those are full portfolio reruns. Execution assumptions can change which trades are accepted, position sizes and subsequent opportunities. They are not just a flat deduction from the primary result. All three use the same historical source, so they are not three independent validations.

# What was tested

1. Reproducibility and accounting. These checks verify saved research outputs; they are not a fresh rerun of the entire suite or an independent audit. Six saved portfolio cases across Vesper 2.0 and 2.1 reconciled to the earlier results. Trade counts, ledger cash, monthly and annual profit, equity endpoints and floating drawdown were checked. Source hashes were checked for changes. I rechecked the saved outputs before preparing this post.

2. Sensitivity and capacity. The completed suite contains 80 runs covering execution, financing, nearby settings, account sizes and leverage assumptions. Small accounts skipped opportunities because the minimum executable lot did not fit. Large accounts encountered volume caps. Performance did not scale perfectly with starting capital.

3. Missed orders. There were 400 full account reruns, using 100 deterministic seeds for each combination of 5 or 10 percent missed orders and primary or harsh execution. All remained profitable over this historical period, but some experienced substantially larger drawdowns. The harsh tests with 10 percent missed orders reached a maximum floating drawdown of 48.70 percent across tested seeds.

4. Random controls. Each accepted main trade was compared with 500 matched random entry timing draws and 500 random direction draws. The observed entry timing did not outperform the matched random timing control. Direction performed better than its random control, but that comparison is conditional on already selected setups and does not prove a general edge.

5. Monte Carlo. The suite used 20,000 resamples per method, including individual months and blocks of consecutive months. These reorder observed historical returns. They do not generate independent market evidence, and their month end drawdowns omit intramonth adverse movement.

# What did not pass a strong robustness standard

Nearby parameter settings reduced modeled profit considerably. Financing assumptions materially changed results. Under extreme execution, Vesper 2.1 made only about $50 more than Vesper 2.0 while taking more drawdown.

Approximately 60.9 percent of primary dollar profit came from the partial 2026 year. Earlier compounding contributes to that dollar concentration, but it still means the headline result depends heavily on a recent period. The primary account also had a losing 2021.

Most importantly, this history and candidate were already used during development. This is not a genuinely untouched holdout, and completing the suite does not mean every robustness test passed.

# My current conclusion

Vesper 2.1 is a promising historical research candidate. The accounting and reproducibility checks passed, but a robust live edge remains unproven. Native broker execution validation and a prospective record with frozen rules are still missing from this evidence package.

I would be interested in feedback on the validation methodology, particularly stronger timing controls, sensitivity testing and ways to measure dependence on one recent market period without retuning the model after seeing the results.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
Since the observed entries did not beat the 500 matched random-timing draws, I would tighten that control before interpreting direction as the edge. Keep Vesper 2.1’s direction, sizing, and management fixed, but move each entry among eligible timestamps matched on session, volatility, spread, and setup duration. That tests timing without giving the placebo easier market conditions.

For the 60.9% of dollar profit from partial 2026, report uncompounded expectancy, profit factor, and drawdown by rolling three-year window, plus the full result with 2026 removed. Freeze those calculations now and carry the same table into native MT5 shadow execution, since compounding makes late-period dollar contribution hard to interpret.

replies.author: symtrader
replies.body:
Thanks, this is a useful distinction. I've now completed a fixed risk, uncompounded analysis of the saved Vesper 2.1 trades, with the rules and original accepted trade cohorts unchanged.

With 2026 entries excluded, the results are:  
Primary: $27,979.45 net profit, $58.17 expectancy per trade, profit factor 1.637.  
Harsh: $19,422.77 net profit, $60.89 expectancy, profit factor 1.442.  
Extreme: $14,495.91 net profit, $47.53 expectancy, profit factor 1.306.

Removing each year individually left a positive remaining total in all three cases. Across 82 overlapping rolling 36 month windows, losing windows were 0 primary, 3 harsh and 12 extreme. These windows group trades by UTC entry month and include their eventual closed outcomes, which can fall after the window. They are not 82 independent tests or simulations liquidated at each window end.

This is attribution on the original accepted trades, not fresh portfolio simulations: it does not recalculate admission, executable lot rounding, monthly sizing or floating equity. I also would not present its closed trade drawdown as the floating percentage drawdown in the original post.

The stricter 500 draw timing test you describe remains incomplete. Actual historical spreads are missing, and the saved history was already used during development. Scenario cost assumptions are not observed spread matching. The existing conditional direction result therefore is not proof of a standalone edge. There is no genuinely untouched period to claim as passed, and the native shadow comparison and prospective frozen record are still pending.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: This is a careful write-up, and it's rare to see the failures listed next to the results. For stronger timing controls, I'd run the same random-timing test on a period that was never used during development, since the entry timing not beating random on the data you tuned on is a warning sign. To measure the dependence on 2026, you could report the result with 2026 removed and with each year removed in turn, without changing any rule. A prospective record with frozen rules, even on paper, is probably the most convincing next step. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and run it in paper mode first, which is a similar way to build that record.

replies.author: symtrader
replies.body:
Thanks, the point about an untouched period is fair. I checked the saved results and can add some context on the 2026 dependence.

Starting from $10,000 in January 2017, the modeled account balances at December 2025 were $117,421.32 under primary execution, $51,658.72 under harsh execution and $31,291.34 under extreme execution. Those are checkpoints from the existing continuous simulations, with their modeled costs and financing. They are not fresh runs deleting a year, resetting capital or forcing all positions closed at that boundary.

In the primary case, partial 2026 added $167,144.33, or 60.88% of the full period's dollar profit. The earlier period was positive overall, but uneven: 2021 lost 7.23% under primary execution. Compounding contributes to the late dollar concentration, so these balances alone do not resolve regime dependence.

On timing, 324 of 500 matched random timing draws equalled or exceeded the observed primary score (empirical upper tail p about 0.649). That comparison was conditional on the already selected trades, not a fresh search over all possible setups, and it was on history already used in development. I agree it does not establish a timing edge.

I don't have a completed untouched period timing test or a full year omission analysis to report here. A prospective record with frozen rules is still missing for this version. The earlier small live experiment is a different version, so I am keeping it separate from this evidence.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Thanks for adding the checkpoints and being clear about what they do and don't show. The 324 of 500 random draws matching or beating the observed score is a useful number to publish. A prospective record with frozen rules is the right next step, and I'll leave it there.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: recording yourself explaining charts before writing any rules is a smart order to do it in. most people go straight to code and only find the ambiguity when the backtest looks odd. when the indicator and your own read disagreed on a candle, which side usually won?

replies.author: symtrader
replies.body:
It wasn’t really about which side won. Sometimes the indicator would flag a setup I’d already ruled out discretionarily, and it would later get invalidated before an entry triggered anyway.  
The interesting part was figuring out what I’d spotted that made me dismiss it earlier. That’s been the hardest part: breaking down those decisions into clear, repeatable rules without adding so many conditions that the system becomes overly complicated.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's the useful part though, the dismissal is a rule you already follow but haven't written down. I'd log every setup you rule out with a one-line reason for a few weeks. the reasons repeat, and two or three of them usually turn into filters you can code.
